description:
How to Email a PhD Supervisor: 7 Templates (2027)

Direct answer box (first 50 words):

Email a UK PhD supervisor with a short (150–200 word), specific message: one line on who you are, two or three sentences showing you have actually read their work, a clear question about whether they are taking students, and your CV attached. Send it Tuesday–Thursday morning; follow up once after two weeks.

Why most "cold emails" to supervisors fail

Supervisors receive dozens of generic enquiries every term. The ones that get deleted share the same faults: they never mention a specific paper or project, they ask the supervisor to "guide me on funding opportunities" (that is your job), and they run to 600 words.

The ones that get replies do three things in under 200 words:

  1. Name the project. Ideally an advertised studentship, or a funding scheme you could realistically bring — our guide to spotting a PhD that is genuinely funded for international students shows how to verify this before you write.
  2. Prove you read their work. One specific sentence beats a paragraph of flattery.
  3. Ask one answerable question. "Are you accepting a PhD student for October 2027 on X topic?" can be answered in five seconds.

Before you send anything, make sure your CV is ready — supervisors often forward promising emails straight to admissions, and a weak CV kills the thread. Our academic CV structure guide with example covers the two-page academic format.

The 7 templates

Adjust the bracketed placeholders and keep every email under 200 words.

Template 1 — First contact about an advertised project

Template 2 — Self-proposed topic (no advert exists)

Template 3 — Asking about funding (before you invest months)

Template 4 — Explaining a gap or weak grade, briefly

One sentence, no excuses, then evidence. If the weakness is bigger than one line, let the evidence carry it: put compensating achievements at the top of your academic CV so the committee reads them first.

Template 5 — Requesting a quick call

Template 6 — After a positive reply / before formal application

Template 7 — After interview or rejection, keeping the door open

Rejections are normal — what you do in the following week matters more. See our guide on what to do after a PhD application is rejected.

Timing, etiquette and follow-up

DoDon't
Send Tue–Thu, 8–10am UK timeSend Friday evening or at 3am local time
Follow up once after 10–14 working daysFollow up twice in a week
Use a university or professional email addressUse an informal personal address
Attach CV + transcript as PDFs, clearly namedAttach 6 files or send a Drive link with no context
CC nobody on first contactCC three supervisors in one email

If a week or two passes with no reply, don't take it personally — inboxes flood during admissions season. Our follow-up guide with a ready template shows exactly when and how to nudge.

Frequently asked questions

How long should an email to a PhD supervisor be? 150–200 words. Long enough to prove you have read their work; short enough to be read on a phone between meetings.

Should I email multiple supervisors at once? Yes, but separately and with individually tailored messages. Never send one identical email to several supervisors, and never CC them together — UK academia is small.

What if I get no reply at all? Send one follow-up after two weeks. If that fails, move on — non-replies usually mean the supervisor is away, full, or the mailbox is unmonitored. Silence is not a judgment on your ability.

Do I need a supervisor before applying to a UK PhD? For most UK PhDs, yes — an informal "yes, I'd support your application" from a supervisor is effectively step one, before the formal portal application. In the Netherlands and much of continental Europe, you apply to an advertised project instead, where the advert itself is the first contact.
